title: Yajnavalkya is leaving
hookLine: the greatest sage in the book tells his wife he's leaving home for good, and offers to split the property
carry: a life moves in four stages
tomorrow: Maitreyi: "what would I do with wealth if it doesn't make me immortal?"
last: THE ATMAN IS WHERE LOVE LIVES.

lines: LET ME DIVIDE WHAT I HAVE.
cards: A kitchen, a long marriage, an ordinary evening. And the husband says: I'm going. Not to another house.
Not to another person. He's leaving the householder's life altogether, to wander with nothing. Before I go, he says, let me divide what I have between you and my other wife, so it's settled.
So begins one of the Brihadaranyaka's great conversations. The man is Yajnavalkya, and today is about what it meant, in his world, to leave.

teach.h: A LEADING VOICE OF THIS UPANISHAD.
teach.b: Yajnavalkya is a leading voice of this Upanishad. Tradition credits him with a whole branch of the Veda, the White Yajurveda, and in a few days you'll watch him take on a room full of rivals.
Here he's at home, with two wives, Maitreyi and Katyayani. That's nearly all this chapter tells us about them.

When the scene is told again later in the book, it adds one line: Maitreyi was one who discussed Brahman, and Katyayani had, in the text's short phrase, a woman's knowledge, words readers interpret in different ways.
The text never tells us what Katyayani thought, or how either of them felt, and it's fair to say so. Why is he leaving?
Hindu tradition later described life in four stages: the student, the householder, the forest dweller, and the renunciant, the sannyasi, who gives up home, property and name, and wanders.
Yajnavalkya is stepping from the second stage toward the last. That's the teaching under today's story: Hinduism sees a life as moving through stages, the ashramas, each with its own duty.
The householder's years of work, family and giving are honored, not a mistake. But later in life, the tradition says, loosen your grip on home and turn toward God.

teach.h: TWO WIVES; THE TEXT SAYS LITTLE MORE.
teach.b: Many Hindu grandparents still live a gentle version of it: more pilgrimage, more prayer, fewer things.
In the retelling, the verb is the one used for going forth into that wandering life.
And notice what he does first.

teach.h: A LIFE MOVES IN FOUR STAGES.
teach.b: He doesn't vanish in the night. He sits down and tries to settle the property fairly. Even leaving everything, he wants to leave well.
What keeps the scene alive is what Maitreyi says next.

how: In Hindu tradition sannyasa is taken by formal vows, often late in life, after which the renunciant leaves home and property behind; the four stages of life are an ideal pattern described in the dharma texts, and the householder's life is honored in its own right.

dividing property fairly before a death

games.q: who's who in the scene — tap the pairs.
p: the second stage: work, family, giving
the other wife; the text says little
the wandering life he's going to

s: this conversation appears twice in the Brihadaranyaka
in book two and again in book four, with small differences.
he first offers to settle his property between his two wives.
the text tells us how Katyayani felt
it's silent about her, and about how either wife felt.

games.q: in the four stages of life, which stage is Yajnavalkya leaving, and which is he heading toward?
o: leaving the householder's life, heading toward the wanderer's.
leaving the student's life, heading toward marriage.
leaving the wanderer's life, heading back home.
games.why: householder to wanderer: the last stage, sannyasa. and before he goes, he sits down to settle his property fairly. then Maitreyi asks a question that changes everything.

practice: Think of something you're getting ready to leave, or will one day: a job, a house, a role, a habit, a stage of life.

Don't decide anything; just ask what Yajnavalkya asked: what would it take to settle this fairly, so the people around it are cared for? Let one small answer come, then let the question go and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Sannyasa, renunciation, laying everything down. He is leaving home for good, and first offers to settle his property between Maitreyi and Katyayani.

orig.note: Sanskrit saṃnyāsa: laying everything down. the fourth and last stage of life in the dharma texts.
